title: New Love
text:
Every new love that appears

illuminates our existence,

perfumes it and makes it flower.


In the densest darkness

every woman is radiance

and every love is clarity.

To cure the stubborn

sorrow hidden in souls,

a new love is effective;

for it settles on our hurt

without ever harming the wound,

like a gleam on crystal.


Like a dream in a cradle,

as on ruin settles

the mercy of a ray of moonlight.

like an enchantment on tedium,

like on the tip of a thorn

a little drop of dew...


That it also knows how to make one suffer?

That it also knows how to make one weep?

That it also knows how to make one die?


—It is that you did not know how to love...
editorial_note: The translation keeps the consoling argument for new love and the sharp closing correction.

title: Because I Still Contemplate Radiant Dawns...
text:
Because I still contemplate radiant dawns

and there are roses, many roses, many roses

where the star of Bethlehem trembles,

and there are roses, many roses, many roses,

thank you, it is well!


Because in the afternoons, with subtle faintness,

the sun piously kisses my temple,

and still transfigures it with its ray:

thank you, it is well!


Because at night a voice calls my name

(the voice of someone I know!), and there is an Eden

hidden in the folds of my shadow:

thank you, it is well!


Because even evil in me is a gift from heaven,

since, as it undermines me, with rough zeal,

it also crumbles my prison;

because my first flight is already drawing near:

thank you, it is well!
editorial_note: This first-line variant keeps the grateful refrain and the prison-to-flight motion.

title: My Secret? It Is So Sad! I Am Lost...
text:
My secret? It is so sad! I am lost

in love with a vanished being,

with a freed soul,

who for ten years was mine, and who has gone...

My secret? I will tell it in your ear:

I am in love with a dead woman!


Do you understand—you who seek the visible

transports, the real, the tangible

caresses of the woman who takes shape

for all your invincible desires—

that impossible of impossibles:

to adore a ghost?


Well, such is my life and such has it been

and will be!

If for me alone

her noble heart beat, now silent and frozen,

must I show myself ungrateful

and forget her, merely because she has departed,

and leave her, merely because she has died?
editorial_note: This first-line variant keeps the whispered confession and ghostly fidelity.

title: I Am Not So Very Wise as to Deny You
text:
I am not so very wise as to deny you,

Lord; I find your divine existence logical;

it is enough for me to open my eyes to find you;

all creation invites me to adore you,

and I adore you in the rose and adore you in the thorn.

What are our anguishes, that we should want to

argue you cruel? Do we perhaps know

if with our tears you make the stars,

if the highest beings, if the most beautiful things

are kneaded with the noble clay of bitterness?

Let us wait, let us suffer, let us never cast

at the Invisible our negation like a challenge.


Poor sad creature, you will see, you will see!

Death draws near... From its lips you will hear

the heavenly secret!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's humble theological logic and its final promise of a secret heard from Death.

title: Afterward
text:
I hate you with the hatred of withered illusion:

Withdraw! I have drunk your chalice, and because of that

my lips no longer know where to place their kiss;

my flesh, tormented by pleasures, dies sated.


Sappho, Chrysis, Aspasia, Magdalene, Aphrodite,

all I ever desired you were to my wicked eagerness.

Where to find spasms, where to find excess

that your accursed perversion does not offer me at once?


Go away! Painful shames invade me,

unspeakable blushes of evil, frank rancors,

on seeing fever tremble over your rosy breasts.


I no longer want the lyre of your flanks to vibrate:

leave me alone and sad to weep for my glorious

virginities dead between your white thighs.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the sonnet's bitter post-pleasure revulsion and mythic catalog of desire.

title: Space and Time
text:
Space and time, bars

of the cage

in which the soul, an enchanted

princess,

is spinning, spinning near

the windows

of the eyes (the only

openings through which

she usually leans out, languid).


Space and time, bars

of the cage;

you will break one day, and perhaps

very soon, because each

month, hour, instant, notches you,

and the golden bird

watches for a crack to spread its wings!


The cunning princess

pretends to spin; but waits

for a bar to break...

Meanwhile, to the distant

stars she says: "Friends,

stretch me your ladder

of light over the abyss."


And the pale stars

answer her: "Wait,

wait, sister,

and ready your efforts:

we are already stretching the ladder!"
editorial_note: The translation keeps the soul as both captive princess and golden bird awaiting release.

title: Renunciation
text:
Oh, Siddhartha Gautama! you were right:

anguishes come to us from desire; Eden

consists in not longing, in the complete,

irrevocable renunciation of all possession;

one who desires nothing is well wherever he is.


Desire is a cup of infinite bitterness,

an octopus of insatiable tentacles, which, as

they are cut, are born again for our torture.

Desire is the father of spleen, of satiety,

and there are more treacheries in it than in the waves of the sea!


Whoever drinks like the Cynic from his hand,

whoever is capable of turning his back on money,

whoever loves the Arcane above all things,

he is the victorious one, the strong, the sovereign...

and no peace compares with his perennial peace!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the Buddhist argument against desire and the closing image of sovereign peace.

title: Via, Veritas et Vita
text:
To see in all things

the traces of the unknown Spirit;

to contemplate

without cease,

in the transparent mysterious nights,

the holy nakedness of the stars...

To wait!

To wait!

What? Who knows! Perhaps a future

and undreamed-of peace... Serene and strong,

to run that sublime

and portentous adventure of death.


Meanwhile, to love everything... and to love nothing,

to smile when there is sun and when there are mists;

to take care that on the harsh journey

the wings do not atrophy, nor any wave

of vile mire soil our feathers.


Soul: such is the best orientation,

such is the instinctive course

shown to us by an inner

star.
editorial_note: The Latin-titled variant keeps the same spiritual course toward death and the inner star.
